subtype: Friend × Asking a friend for money [Actor]
passage:
"Kavitha, can I ask you something awkward?"
"That face means money."
"It does. My hostel fee is due Friday and my stipend is late. Could I borrow some for two weeks? I'll return it on the tenth, when the stipend comes."
"How much?"
"The exact balance. I'll show you the number, and I'll put the date in our shared notes so neither of us forgets."
"Okay. Thanks for asking straight. I hate it when people go silent and then dodge me."
"I'd hate that too. I nearly waited until Thursday because I was embarrassed 😅."
"Shalini, just ask sooner next time."

On the tenth, Shalini sent the money at breakfast, before Kavitha had even remembered.

qa.q: When did Shalini promise to repay the money?
qa.a: On the tenth, when the stipend comes.

qa.q: What was Shalini worried about before asking?
qa.a: Being embarrassed. Shalini nearly waited until Thursday to bring it up.

qa.q: What made Shalini's request work well?
qa.a: Shalini asked clearly, named the repayment date, offered to write it down and then actually repaid on time.

qa.q: How does Kavitha feel about being asked directly?
qa.a: Kavitha says asking straight is better than people going silent and dodging, so a clear request makes it easy to say yes. 🙂

grounding: Shalini is short of money, asks a friend clearly, names a repayment date and repays.

passage:
At nine at night, with a viva the next morning, Arnab's phone lit up with a message from a batchmate: "Is it true you're quitting engineering? Sorry to hear that." The only person he had told was Kalyani. His face went hot.

He wanted to type something cruel. He even opened the note where he kept what Kalyani had once confided about her failed paper, then closed it. Instead he wrote to her: "Can we talk after the viva? Just us."

The next day, on the library steps, he said, "I told only you. Now half the class knows. I'm angry, and I want to know what happened." Kalyani stared at her shoes. "I told one person. I didn't think it would go anywhere." Arnab nodded slowly. He didn't hug her. From now on he would share smaller things and watch what came back.

qa.q: When was Arnab's viva?
qa.a: The next morning.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he read the message, and what did he nearly do?
qa.a: Angry and exposed, with his face hot. He nearly used Kalyani's own confided secret against her but closed the note.

qa.q: What did Arnab do wisely in this situation?
qa.a: He waited until after the viva, asked to talk privately, told Kalyani how he felt and did not leak her secret in return.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt on the library steps?
qa.a: Ashamed or defensive. She stared at her shoes and said she didn't think it would go anywhere.

grounding: Arnab's secret spreads; he feels exposed and furious, confronts Kalyani privately and decides how much to trust her.

passage:
I'm Lata, and I live next to Chandrika's room, so I heard most of it.

On Monday at dinner, Chandrika was the centre of the table, telling everyone that Amandeep had been failing calculus and hiding it from home. People laughed a little, then went quiet when one of Amandeep's friends looked over. Chandrika's laugh trailed off.

Later that night I heard her at Amandeep's door. No excuses, as far as I could tell. "I told them your thing. I wanted them to listen to me. It was wrong, and I'm sorry." Amandeep said, "I need some space right now." Chandrika said, "Okay. I understand," and went back to her room.

I can't say what either of them felt. I only know Chandrika skipped breakfast for two days.

qa.q: What did Chandrika tell the table about Amandeep?
qa.a: That Amandeep had been failing calculus and hiding it from home.

qa.q: What might Chandrika's trailing laugh suggest, and why can't Lata be sure?
qa.a: It might suggest Chandrika felt caught or uneasy when Amandeep's friend looked over. Lata only saw behaviour and cannot know the inner state for sure.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that a wise person would?
qa.a: Owned it quickly, apologised without excuses and accepted Amandeep's request for space.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt hearing this at the door?
qa.a: Probably exposed and hurt, and asking for space suggests trust will need time to come back, if it does.

grounding: Chandrika shared a friend's confidence for attention, then owned it and apologised without excuses, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
For three weeks I rehearsed what I would say to Neelam. My name is Gargi, and I don't let things go easily. Neelam had presented my poster idea to the fest committee as her own, and I found out from a stranger. I lost sleep, checked her stories and went cold with her in the corridor.

Then one evening on the terrace she said sorry, properly, without a "but". I noticed my shoulders drop. I told her, "I forgive you. That's for me, honestly, I'm tired of carrying it. But I'm not going to share unfinished ideas with you for a while." She nodded and said that was fair.

I didn't pretend it never happened. Our tea afterwards was quieter than before, and I was fine with that.

qa.q: How did Gargi find out about the poster idea?
qa.a: From a stranger.

qa.q: Why did Gargi say the forgiveness was for herself?
qa.a: Because Gargi was tired of carrying the hurt. Gargi's shoulders dropped once the apology came.

qa.q: Why is forgiving while keeping a limit wiser than pretending nothing happened?
qa.a: It lets Gargi find peace now, while trust can be rebuilt slowly or not at all, without ignoring what Neelam did.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt when Gargi set the limit?
qa.a: Perhaps disappointed but accepting. Neelam nodded and called it fair.

grounding: Gargi chooses to forgive a friend who hurt her for her own peace, without fully restoring trust.

passage:
Sudha was shelling peas on the verandah when her phone buzzed: a group photo from the riverbank, six friends with jalebi and a cricket bat, Tanvir grinning in the middle. Nobody had told her about it. The peas went into the bowl faster, and her throat felt tight. So they don't want me now, she thought.

She put the phone down, finished the peas and listened to a bus honking on the main road. Then she picked it up again and typed to Tanvir: "Saw the riverbank photos. It stung a bit that I wasn't there. Was it planned for a reason?"

Tanvir called within minutes. "It was Rafiq's cousin's plan, and we got roped in at the bus stand. I should have called you. Come next Sunday, we're going again."

Sudha smiled at the peas, still stung, but lighter.

qa.q: What were the friends holding in the riverbank photo?
qa.a: Jalebi and a cricket bat.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel on seeing the photo, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt hurt and left out, thinking her friends no longer wanted her; her throat felt tight and the peas went into the bowl faster.

qa.q: What did Sudha do that helped, compared with assuming the worst?
qa.a: She let herself feel the sting, then asked Tanvir directly and calmly, which gave room for a kinder explanation.

qa.q: How did Tanvir see the gathering?
qa.a: As an unplanned outing that came together at the bus stand, and Tanvir regretted not calling Sudha.

grounding: Sudha sees photos of a gathering she was not invited to, feels the sting, and asks directly instead of assuming malice.

subtype: Friend × Taking sides in a conflict [Actor]
passage:
Pranav: You saw what Neha posted about me. Whose side are you on?
Ishita: I saw it. Posting it in the group was unkind.
Pranav: So you agree with me!
Ishita: Not fully. Dropping out of Neha's birthday plan without telling anyone wasn't fair either.
Pranav: Wow. So you're on her side.
Ishita: I'm not on a side. I told Neha the same thing this morning. You both did something that hurt the other.
Pranav: That's not helping 😠
Ishita: I know it's annoying to hear. I'm still here, and I'll help you write her an honest message if you want.
Pranav: ...let me think.
Ishita: Take your time 🙂

qa.q: What did Ishita say she had told Neha that morning?
qa.a: The same thing she was telling Pranav: that both had done something that hurt the other.

qa.q: What is Pranav feeling in this chat, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Angry and frustrated. Pranav wants Ishita to agree and answers "That's not helping" with an angry face.

qa.q: How does Ishita say what she thinks is right without hurting either friend?
qa.a: She names what was unkind on both sides, offers to help with an honest message, and says she is still there.

qa.q: How might Neha see Ishita's stance?
qa.a: Neha may be relieved that Ishita is not attacking behind Neha's back, or a little stung to hear their own part named.

grounding: Ishita is pressed to choose sides and states what she thinks is right about both without gossiping to either.

subtype: Friend × Being used for notes, money or contacts [Receiver]
passage:
I'm Nazia, and it took me a whole semester to see the pattern. Bidisha called at odd hours: the night before submissions for my notes, before a trip for my cousin's contact at a travel agency, on the fifteenth for a small loan. When I had nothing to give, her messages went quiet. I said yes every time because I was scared she'd stop liking me, and I even bought her coffee to keep things warm.

One evening I noticed I felt used, and also that I still cared about her. So I did something small. "I'll share my notes today, but I can't do it every time. And I'd love to just hang out sometime with no favours." She looked surprised. "Oh. I didn't realise." We're not as close as before, but I help when I want to, and it feels cleaner.

qa.q: What did Bidisha ask for before a trip?
qa.a: Nazia's cousin's contact at a travel agency.

qa.q: Why did Nazia keep saying yes at first?
qa.a: Out of fear that Bidisha would stop liking Nazia, so Nazia even bought coffee to keep things warm.

qa.q: What limit did Nazia set, and how did it help?
qa.a: Nazia offered notes that day, said it could not be every time, and invited a no-favours hangout. It was clear without bitterness.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have seen the pattern?
qa.a: Possibly without noticing it. Bidisha's "Oh. I didn't realise" suggests surprise rather than deliberate use.

grounding: Nazia realises a friend calls only when she needs something, and sets limits without bitterness.

passage:
Mentor's note, week five. In group project meetings I have seen Indu correct Payal's English in front of everyone and roll her eyes when Payal spoke about her school in a small town. Payal has gone quiet and now sends her slides by message instead of presenting.

I asked Indu to stay after class. She was defensive at first: "I'm only being honest." When I asked what she was afraid of, she was silent, then said her first-semester marks were poor and everyone else seemed to speak better than her. It felt good, she admitted, to have someone she could look down on.

I did not scold her. I suggested she read Payal's slides properly before the next meeting. This week Indu asked Payal about her data, and I saw Payal present again. I will keep watching.

qa.q: What did Payal start doing instead of presenting?
qa.a: Sending her slides by message.

qa.q: What did Indu's answer show about her feelings behind the eye-rolling?
qa.a: Insecurity. Indu feared being behind and said it felt good to have someone to look down on.

qa.q: How did the mentor help without lecturing?
qa.a: They asked what Indu was afraid of, did not scold, and suggested reading Payal's slides properly.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt in the meetings before this?
qa.a: Embarrassed and small. Going quiet suggests Payal was avoiding more corrections in front of everyone.

grounding: Indu looks down on Payal for background and English; the contempt is traced to insecurity and Indu begins to treat Payal as an equal.

passage:
I'm Irawati, and I sit behind Sarika in Hindi lit. Every break, three girls copy her accent: "Sarika, say 'water' again!" They laugh at her salwar and call her "village girl" as if it were a pet name. Sarika laughs too, but her ears go red and she stares at her tiffin.

On Thursday she said, in a flat voice, "It isn't funny to me anymore. Please stop." One of them said, "We're just joking." Sarika said, "I know. It still hurts."

The teasing didn't stop straight away. The next week Sarika ate lunch on the steps with Anita and me, where nobody mimics anyone. I can't tell how much it stings inside, because she doesn't say much. But she talks more when she's there.

qa.q: What did the three girls call Sarika?
qa.a: "Village girl".

qa.q: What might Sarika's red ears and staring at her tiffin suggest, and why can't we be sure?
qa.a: They may suggest discomfort or hurt hidden behind the laughing, but Irawati only sees the outside and cannot know for sure.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that helped in the end?
qa.a: Sarika told them it hurt, and when the teasing continued, moved lunch to kinder company.

qa.q: How might the three girls have seen the teasing before Thursday?
qa.a: As harmless jokes. Their reply "We're just joking" suggests they did not think it was hurting Sarika.

grounding: Friends constantly tease Sarika for accent, clothes and small-town origin; she says it hurts and finds kinder people, seen by an observer.

passage:
I'm Charu, Rekha's roommate, and I saw the change before Rekha said a word.

In the canteen on Tuesday the usual group was joking about Sameer's old laptop with its cracked corner, and how he "must be selling it soon". Rekha laughed loudly, the way you laugh to belong.

Two days later, at the placement workshop, someone joked about the borrowed blazer Rekha wore, sleeves too long. Rekha smiled, then went to the washroom and stayed a while. That evening Rekha said, to nobody in particular, "Being the joke is awful."

On Friday, when the group started on Sameer again, Rekha said, "I'll pass, that's getting old," and picked up a tray. Nobody answered. I can't say what Rekha felt, but Rekha then walked over to Sameer's table and asked about the laptop stickers.

qa.q: What did the group joke about Sameer?
qa.a: His old laptop with its cracked corner, and that he "must be selling it soon".

qa.q: How did Rekha seem to feel after the joke about the borrowed blazer, and what is uncertain?
qa.a: Hurt, judging by the smile followed by a long stay in the washroom and the remark "Being the joke is awful". Charu cannot be sure of Rekha's inner state.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that a wise friend might do?
qa.a: Rekha quietly refused to join in with "I'll pass, that's getting old" and then reached out to Sameer.

qa.q: How might Sameer have felt about the jokes and Rekha's later question?
qa.a: Probably stung by the canteen jokes, and a friendly question about the stickers may feel like being seen as more than the joke.

grounding: Rekha laughs along at Sameer's expense to fit in, feels what it is like to be the joke, and quietly refuses, seen by a roommate.
